title: Leaving Laban (Genesis 31)
hookLine: twenty hard years, stolen idols, and a heap of stones as a boundary of peace

cards: Twenty years in Laban's house, and the mood has turned. Jacob came with a walking stick; now he has two wives, eleven sons, a daughter and huge flocks. Laban's sons grumble that Jacob got rich off their father.
Laban's face, the Torah says, isn't toward him as it used to be. The welcome has quietly run out. Then God speaks: go back to the land of your fathers, and I will be with you.
Jacob calls Rachel and Leah out to the field. And the two sisters, rivals until now, speak with one voice: our father has treated us like strangers. Whatever God told you, do it.

teach.b: While Laban is away shearing sheep, Jacob loads everything onto camels and slips away.

teach.h: THE IDOLS END UP SAT ON.
teach.b: Rachel, without telling him, takes her father's household idols. Laban chases them for seven days and catches up in the hills of Gilead, but God has warned him in a dream: be careful what you say to Jacob.
Rachel has hidden them in her camel's saddle; when Laban searches every tent for his stolen gods, she sits on them and apologizes that she can't get up.
So the household gods, the kind Abram walked away from long ago, end up sat on. Rashi, the medieval commentator, says she took them to pull her father away from idol worship.

teach.h: MY SLEEP FLED FROM MINE EYES.
teach.b: Then Jacob lets out twenty years of anger, in the old JPS translation: "in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep fled from mine eyes." You changed my wages ten times, he says.
But the story doesn't end in a fight. It ends in a pile of stones. Jacob sets up a pillar, the family heaps stones, and they eat there by the heap.
Laban names it in Aramaic, Jegar-sahadutha; Jacob names it in Hebrew, Galeed.
Two languages, one meaning: a heap of witness.

teach.h: THE LORD WATCH BETWEEN ME AND THEE.
teach.b: Laban adds: "The LORD watch between me and thee, when we are absent one from another." The heap is a line. I won't cross it to harm you, and you won't cross it to harm me.
Not friendship. Not love. A boundary, set in stone, so that peace can hold.

how: Jews read Jacob's departure from Laban in the Torah portion Vayetze; Laban's words at the heap give the place a second name, Mizpah, the watchpost (Genesis 31:49).

Jacob running from Esau's anger by night

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: hid the household idols in a saddle
how often Laban changed the wages

s: Jacob knew Rachel had taken her father's idols
she took them without telling him, and hid them in her camel's saddle.
the heap of stones got names in two languages
Laban called it Jegar-sahadutha in Aramaic; Jacob called it Galeed in Hebrew. both mean heap of witness.
the heap marked a friendship pact
it marked a boundary: neither would cross it to harm the other.

games.q: you're Jacob. Laban has caught up with you after seven days, angry, and searched every tent. what happens next?
o: you fight, and part as enemies.
you set up a heap of stones as a boundary, and eat together.
you go back to Laban's house.
games.why: after Jacob's angry speech, they heap up stones, eat on them, and agree: neither will cross this line to harm the other.

practice: Think of a relationship where something keeps getting crossed: a relative who drops by unannounced, a boss who texts at midnight.

You don't have to end anything; picture a small heap of stones between you, a clear, calm line, and say silently, kindly, the one sentence that would set it, like: I can talk after dinner, not during.
If you pray, you can ask for a steady voice.

wordCard.voice: Leaving Laban: twenty hard years, stolen idols, and a heap of stones that keeps the peace.

orig.note: Hebrew: a heap of witness. Jacob's name for the boundary heap.

carryVoice: Your line: a heap of witness. A clear line can be its own kind of kindness. Day sixty: two months.
